name: Aorto-Right Ventricular Tunnel

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: No formal consensus criteria; diagnosis based on imaging and clinical findings

criteria.description: Identification of an abnormal tunnel-like communication between the aorta and right ventricle on echocardiography or cardiac MRI
Presence of continuous cardiac murmur and signs of volume overload or heart failure in infancy or early childhood
Exclusion of other congenital heart defects such as ventricular septal defect or ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All three major criteria including imaging confirmation, clinical presentation, and exclusion of other defects
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis relies heavily on imaging modalities and clinical correlation; no standardized diagnostic scoring system exists.

pathognomonic.notes: Typically loud and best heard at the left upper sternal border
searchTerms: heart murmur present all the time

pathognomonic.notes: Signs include tachypnea, hepatomegaly, and poor feeding

common.notes: May present as fatigue or dyspnea on exertion in older children
Common in infants with significant shunting
May be reported in older children

occasional.notes: Secondary to increased pulmonary blood flow

rare.notes: Rare but reported in untreated cases
Due to arrhythmia or decreased cardiac output

laboratory: Elevated brain natriuretic peptide (BNP) in heart failure
Normal inflammatory markers unless endocarditis present
imaging: Echocardiography showing tunnel-like communication between aorta and right ventricle
Cardiac MRI or CT angiography confirming anatomy and shunt size
Chest X-ray showing cardiomegaly and pulmonary congestion
genetic: No specific genetic mutations identified; sporadic congenital anomaly
other: Cardiac catheterization may be used for hemodynamic assessment and surgical planning

distinguishingFeatures: VSD presents with a defect in the interventricular septum rather than a tunnel from aorta to right ventricle
Different murmur characteristics and echocardiographic findings
Ruptured sinus of Valsalva aneurysm causes acute left-to-right shunt with different clinical presentation
Typically presents later in life and associated with aneurysmal dilation

redFlags: Signs of congestive heart failure in neonate or infant
Sudden onset of severe cardiac symptoms or collapse
Continuous murmur with signs of volume overload
references: Mavroudis C, Backer CL. Pediatric Cardiac Surgery. 4th ed. Elsevier; 2013.
Gatzoulis MA, et al. Diagnosis and Management of Congenital Heart Disease. 2nd ed. Elsevier; 2017.
